entries.title: US: FDA recalls 19 million eggs over Salmonella risk
entries.summary: The US has issued a serious health warning over the recalled eggs, saying exposure to the potentially contaminated products could cause severe illness or death.
entries.content:
August 15, 2026

The US has issued a serious health warning over the recalled eggs, saying exposure to the potentially contaminated products could cause severe illness or death.

Around 19 million eggs have been recalled in the United States over possible Salmonella contamination, the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has said.

Midwest Poultry Services (MPS) voluntarily recalled 1,589,577 dozen eggs on July 22 after detecting potential Salmonella Enteritidis contamination at two Texas farms, the FDA said.

MPS Egg Farms said on its website that it had proactively recalled the eggs as a precautionary measure and initiated testing protocols to identify potential sources of Salmonella.

On Wednesday, the FDA said it was a Class 1 recall, indicating a reasonable probability of serious illness or death.

What did the FDA say about the egg recall?

The eggs were produced between June 6 and July 3 and distributed in the states of Texas, Oklahoma, Arkansas, Louisiana, New Mexico and Mississippi.

These included both white shell eggs and brown cage-free shell eggs.

They were sold under several brand names, with sell-by or best-by dates from July 20 to August 17.

According to the FDA advisory:

  • Consumers should throw away the recalled eggs or return them for a refund
  • Restaurants and retailers should not serve or sell the eggs
  • Consumers, restaurants, and retailers who purchased or received recalled eggs should carefully clean and sanitize any surfaces or containers that the recalled eggs touched.

entries.title: Indonesia: Strong earthquake hits off coast of Flores island
entries.summary: At least five people have died and several buildings were damaged after the powerful magnitude 7.7 earthquake, which was followed by dozens of aftershocks. A tsunami warning has been lifted.
entries.content:
August 15, 2026

At least five people have died and several buildings were damaged after the powerful magnitude 7.7 earthquake, which was followed by dozens of aftershocks. A tsunami warning has been lifted.

A powerful earthquake struck off the coast of Indonesia early on Saturday, killing at least five people, authorities said.

Preliminary reports show two deaths in Sikka Regency and three in Manggarai Regency, authorities said.

The epicenter of the magnitude 7.7 earthquake hit off the coast of the island of Flores at a shallow depth of 10 kilometers (6.2 miles), the US Geological Survey (USGS) said.

Shallow earthquakes (up to 70 kilometers deep) are considered more dangerous and destructive.

Tsunami waves of less than 1 meter (3 feet) were recorded in several areas of the country before the warning was lifted about three hours after the quake.

Where did the earthquake strike?

Indonesia's Meteorology, Climatology, and Geophysics Agency (BMKG) recorded the first quake at 4:58 am (2158 GMT) at a depth of 15 km (9 ⁠miles), followed by dozens of aftershocks.

Video shared on social media from Maumere, the main town in Sikka Regency on Flores Island in eastern Indonesia, showed part of a building collapsing in a cloud of dust and rubble as people screamed and ran into the street.

"Many buildings here were damaged ... I saw that the waiting room at the Pelni port terminal in Maumere had collapsed," Yohanna Embu, a resident of Sikka, a regency within East Nusa Tenggara province, told AP.

Residents evacuated, tsunami warning lifted

The initial jolt was followed by a series of aftershocks in the same area, including one of magnitude 6.1.

BMKG issued a tsunami warning for part of East Nusa Tenggara, West Nusa Tenggara, South Sulawesi and Southeast Sulawesi provinces, urging residents to stay away from beaches and riverbanks.

The tsunami warning was later lifted.

"We have ended (the tsunami warning) but we will keep monitoring the sea level," Wijayanto, earthquake and tsunami director at BMKG, said.

Before the tsunami warning was lifted, residents of Maumere on Flores Island were told to move to higher ground, according to AFP.

State television also showed hundreds of people evacuating in nearby Nagekeo regency.

Local TV footage showed a hospital in the district of Ende in East Nusa Tenggara Province moving patients outside.

Authorities assessing damage, casualties

The quake caused severe damage and collapsed buildings, causing power outages in cities and villages, severely hindering rescue operations.

"We are continuing to collect reports of damages and casualties, but there are communication disruptions," East Nusa Tenggara police chief Rudi Darmoko said.

Local television reports showed patients at several hospitals being evacuated from buildings as a precaution.

"Our students and nuns ran out in panic beneath a collapsing roof," Guidelbertus Tanga, rector of Ritapiret Seminary on Flores said. "At least one priest suffered a broken leg after jumping from the second floor of a building during the quake."

There were also damages reported in some part of southern Sulawesi island.

Indonesia's history of earthquakes

Indonesia is located on the so-called "Ring of Fire," a region of heightened seismic activity in the Pacific basin that stretches from Southeast Asia to Japan.

Here are some of the biggest earthquakes to strike the region:

  • 1992, magnitude 7: A tsunami following a strong earthquake on the southeastern island of Flores killed about 2,500 people
  • 2004, magnitude 9.1: A quake struck off the coast of Sumatra triggering a tsunami that killed 170,000 in Indonesia and 220,000 in several countries in the Indian Ocean
  • 2018, magnitude 6.9: A tremor killed more than 550 people on the islands of Lombok and Sumbawa
  • 2018, magnitude 7.5: A quake and a subsequent tsunami in Palu on Sulawesi island left more than 4,300 people dead or missing

Edited by: Karl Sexton

entries.title: Donald Trump to declare Hormuz US territory 'soon'
entries.summary: Donald Trump said the strait would become part of the US after Iran is defeated. He also told Americans to accept higher gas prices, which have soared since Iran closed Hormuz in response to US and Israeli attacks.
entries.content:
United States of America

Iran war: Trump to declare Hormuz US territory 'soon'

August 15, 2026

Donald Trump said the strait would become part of the US after Iran is defeated. He also told Americans to accept higher gas prices, which have soared since Iran closed Hormuz in response to US and Israeli attacks.

President Donald Trump said Friday that he would "soon" declare the Strait of Hormuz a US territory.

"After we finish defeating Iran, which is being very badly defeated — pretty soon I'll be declaring the Hormuz Strait a territory of the United States," Trump said at a rally at a police academy in Garden City, New York state. "It's true," he added.

It was not clear whether his remarks were serious or whether they signal a new policy shift for Washington in its war against Tehran, which is more than five months old.

Iran's Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi dismissed Trump's remarks, saying the country would "not be intimidated" and that the strategic waterway would remain under its control and authority.

What is the situation in the Strait of Hormuz?

The US and Israel launched the war against Iran on February 28. At the time, senior White House officials, including Trump, said the aim was to end Iran's nuclear program and spark a popular uprising to force regime change in the Islamic Republic, among other goals.

Iran's response has been to target US allies across the Middle East with drone and missile strikes, as well as to impose a blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, through which one-fifth of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG) shipments passed before the war.

The US responded to Iran's closure of the strait with its own naval blockade of Iranian ships and ports. The two countries have been locked in a stalemate over the vital waterway for months, causing energy prices to soar.

Rising oil and gas costs and the economic fallout from the war are likely to be leading issues in the midterm elections in November.

What else did Trump say during the rally in Garden City?

During the rally, the US president also urged Americans to accept that they would have to "pay a tiny little bit more" for their gasoline as a worthy price for preventing "a very evil country" from getting a nuclear weapon.

"What we're doing is a great service for the world, not only for ourselves ... and we're really doing a ​great job," Trump told the crowd, adding that "no ships get through (the US blockade of Hormuz) unless we want them to."

On Friday, Trump also dismissed concerns over the living conditions aboard a US aircraft carrier that was deployed to the Middle East amid the war with Iran.

Relatives of service members aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln told US military media outlets that personnel are struggling with difficult living conditions and deteriorating mental health. There have also been reports of suicide attempts.

Trump denied that the deployment of the aircraft carrier , which has been at sea for nine months, had lasted too long, instead insisting that the aircraft carrier's deployment was "not nearly enough."

He also confirmed that the ship would be replaced by another "very similar" vessel.

Edited by: Louis Oelofse

entries.title: Trump asks Supreme Court to let White House ballroom construction continue
entries.summary: Justice Department lawyers echoed the US president's claim that the $400 million White House ballroom ​project is a security necessity.
entries.content:
United States of America

Trump asks Supreme Court to allow ballroom project

August 15, 2026

Justice Department lawyers echoed the US president's claim that the $400 million White House ballroom ​project is a security necessity.

The Trump administration on Friday asked the US Supreme Court to allow construction to continue on the president's $400 million White House ballroom.

It comes a week after an appeals court ruled Donald Trump's ballroom project, planned for the site of the White House's East Wing after it was demolished, lacked congressional approval and ordered above-ground construction to stop.

"This case involves an extraordinary and unlawful injunction that will halt the ongoing construction of the integrated military complex, including a totally secure ballroom space, at the East Wing of the White House, which is vitally required by national security," Trump's Solicitor General D. John Sauer wrote in a petition to the Supreme Court.

Chief Justice John Roberts set a deadline of Tuesday for a response by plaintiffs challenging the ballroom project.

Trump assassination attempts and flight from Turkey mentioned

The nonprofit National Trust for Historic Preservation first brought the case after the East Wing was torn down and work began on a 90,000-square-foot (8,360-square-meter) ballroom.

In a 2-1 ruling on August 7, the DC Circuit upheld a lower-court judge's order directing the administration to halt above-ground construction.

"Whether or not a massive ballroom should be constructed is for Congress to decide and is not a matter for Executive self-help," the appeals court panel wrote.

To justify the need for a secure ballroom, Justice Department lawyers pointed to the July 8 missile threat against Air Force One when Trump was flown out of Turkey aboard a secret flight and other recent assassination attempts.

The filing also claims the project is on time and under budget, funded by about $400 million in private donations. Democrats, however, say Trump's tax law is helping pay for the ballroom, while lawmakers in Congress have not approved a request by the administration for additional funding.

Responding to the petition, the trust accused the White House of trying to "outrun the courts" by accelerating construction. It cited plans to install 1 million pounds (453,592.37 kilograms) of rebarand pour 3,000 cubic yards (81,000 cubic feet, 2,293.66 cubic meters) of concrete over the next week.

"The Administration's transparent efforts to evade the rule of law, frustrate judicial review, and limit the availability of meaningful relief in the courts must stop here," the plaintiffs said.

The National Trust has urged the Supreme Court to reject the administration's appeal.

Edited by: Karl Sexton

entries.title: Jason Arday: Ex-Cambridge professor at centre of plagiarism scandal found dead
entries.summary: Jason Arday, the youngest ever Black professor at Cambridge, was found unresponsive at an address in London. Arday had recently resigned in the midst of a plagiarism row.
entries.content:
United Kingdom

Jason Arday: Ex-Cambridge professor found dead

August 14, 2026

Jason Arday, the youngest ever Black professor at Cambridge, was found unresponsive at an address in London. Arday had recently resigned in the midst of a plagiarism row.

Jason Arday, the former University of Cambridge professor who resigned amid allegations of plagiarism, was found dead on Friday.

Without naming him directly, the Metropolitan Police said he was found "unresponsive" in Battersea, south London, and pronounced dead at the scene.

"At this time his death is being treated as unexpected, but is not believed to be suspicious," a spokesperson said. "His next-of-kin have been informed and are being supported by officers."

Arday, a professor of sociology of education at Cambridge, one of the world's top universities, resigned just over a week ago amid mounting allegations that he plagiarized parts of his PhD thesis and overstated his personal achievements.

He had denied wrongdoing, saying in a resignation letter last week that he did not accept "the narratives that have surrounded me."

Questions mounted over thesis and fundraising claims

British newspapers and commentators have seized on the allegations, arguing that he gained an unfair advantage through diversity, equality and inclusion (DEI) policies.

Scrutiny of Arday's credentials intensified last month after criticism from former Cambridge researcher Nathan Cofnas.

The Times of London later reported similarities between passages in Arday's 2015 PhD thesis and an earlier paper by another researcher.

Cambridge initially stood by Arday, saying that the plagiarism allegations had been investigated and cleared by Liverpool John Moores University, which awarded Arday's doctorate.

But last week, Cambridge launched an investigation following "new information about Professor Arday's qualifications and honorary appointments."

British media also questioned Arday's claims of having raised £5.5 million (€6.4 million, $7.4 million) for charity through endurance challenges. Arday told The Guardian the funds were raised collectively over two decades.

Supporters reject claims, cite racial bias

Supporters, including over two dozen academics and politicians, characterized the plagiarism allegations as a "smear campaign" designed to discredit Arday and other Black people in influential positions.

In his resignation letter, Arday said that "the relentless accusations, speculation and public commentary have taken a profound toll on me and on those I love."

His family issued a statement denouncing the "campaign of sustained abuse" Arday had faced since he took the role at Cambridge University more than three years ago.

"The campaign of misinformation was too much for Jason, who was a gentle man and who always wanted to see the best in everyone," Arday's family said.

"We won't comment further at this point beyond asking the press to leave us alone now, and to stop the campaign of harassment which has been waged against Jason and his family for too long," the statement added.

Cambridge's Vice-Chancellor Professor Deborah Prentice said, "We are desperately saddened to hear this tragic news. Our heartfelt sympathies go to Jason Arday's family and friends at this incredibly difficult time."

Edited by: Rob Turner and Karl Sexton

entries.title: Vast German wildfire forces evacuation in Eifel forest
entries.summary: Firefighters tackling the biggest forest fire in the history of North Rhine-Westphalia say residents are unlikely to be able to return on Friday amid high temperatures, humidity and wind. DW has the latest.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany: Vast wildfire forces evacuation in Eifel forest

Published August 14, 2026last updated August 14, 2026

Firefighters tackling the biggest forest fire in the history of North Rhine-Westphalia say residents are unlikely to be able to return on Friday amid high temperatures, humidity and wind. DW has the latest.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • A wildfire near the Belgian border has forced about 1,800 people to leave their homes
  • Authorities say residents will not be able to return to their homes overnight
  • Flames burned within 400 meters of one village
  • Police have launched an appeal for information on the cause of the blaze
  • It is the biggest forest fire in the history of Germany's most-populous state, North Rhine-Westphalia

Don't let the algorithm hide the news. If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google so you'll always see our verified news first.

Skip next section Pausing our coverage

Pausing our coverage

We're putting this blog on hold for now, but it will reopen over the weekend with the latest developments.

Skip next section RECAP — Massive wildfire hits Hürtgenwald area, nearby village to stay empty overnight

RECAP — Massive wildfire hits Hürtgenwald area, nearby village to stay empty overnight

In case you're just joining us, here's the lowdown on developments in Germany's far west near the Belgian border this Friday.

A large forest fire in the Hürtgenwald forest, not far east of Aachen, forced authorities to clear a nearby village early in the morning.

Various emergency services and the military have rushed to the area to try to contain almost certainly the largest such blaze in the history of the state of North Rhine-Westphalia, thought to cover an area of at least 200 hectares.

Authorities said on Friday that around 400 personnel were in service simultaneously across various agencies.

The village of Gey, home to around 2,000 people, will remain evacuated overnight. Five people, four of them rescue workers, have suffered injuries amid the response to the fire.

The state premier has cut short his vacation and expects to arrive on site on Saturday afternoon.

Emergency services anticipate that efforts to contain the fire will last all weekend, and perhaps longer. Hot summer weather and a dry forest floor are not helping the response.

Weather forecasts do point to falling temperatures over the weekend, and even a roughly 50% chance of light rain in the area on Saturday.

Police are investigating the cause and have appealed to the public for information, particularly photos or videos from the area taken around the time the fire began.

Skip next section Interior Minister Dobrindt calls fire 'shocking,' praises rescuers

Interior Minister Dobrindt calls fire 'shocking,' praises rescuers

Federal Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt called the images of Friday's forest fire "shocking" and voiced thanks to local and federal first responders alike for their contributions.

"All emergency services are performing exceptionally in the toughest conditions, to fight the flames, protect people, and limit damages. As well as firefighters, state police and the military, the federal police is in operation with its airborne units and the THW [Germany's federal civil protection agency, made up largely of volunteers, that assists in emergency situations] is helping with logistics and operational coordination," Dobrindt said.

Dobrindt's ministry had similarly listed the efforts by various services in a social media post earlier on Friday.

It also noted that there were "several localized vegetation fires" dotted around the country in various states — North Rhine-Westphalia, Rhineland-Palatinate, Saarland and Saxony — on Friday, but said that, with the exception of Hürtgenwald, they were "for the most part under control and have been almost completely extinguished by regional responders."

Skip next section 5 injured amid fire: 4 rescue workers and 1 elderly resident

5 injured amid fire: 4 rescue workers and 1 elderly resident

Local politician Christian Nolten has told the dpa news agency that five people have suffered injuries amid Friday's evacuation and firefighting efforts.

One elderly man suffered a heart complaint during the operations to clear the village of Gey, Nolten said.

And four rescue workers sustained light injuries, such as cuts and circulatory problems, amid their work.

The public gathering point for those affected has been moved further away from the site of the fire, to a special needs school in Düren, for people's safety.

Two initial gathering points closer to the fire have since been closed because of a buildup of smoke and ash in the area.

The next village of Grosshau, to the south of Gey and the heart of the fire, has not yet been evacuated. Düren's Mayor Stephan Cranen said that authorities currently hoped this step would not be necessary, but noted that the situation was still considered fluid and subject to change.

Skip next section Rescue official tells reporters village of Gey will remain cleared overnight

Rescue official tells reporters village of Gey will remain cleared overnight

One of the leading rescue officials in the area, Wilfried Thielen, has told the Kölner Stadt-Anzeiger (KSTA) newspaper that the village of Gey will remain evacuated overnight.

"The Gey settlement has been evacuated. And for safety reasons, we will not allow residents to return tonight," Thielen told the KSTA.

He said that the situation remained fluid, to such an extent that rescue teams were having to reposition their own facilities.

"We've just had to dismantle our staging area because it, too, is at risk because of the changing weather conditions," he said. "This means we're reorganizing, redeploying our personnel and planning our next steps."

Thielen said that authorities had already planned for personnel deployments on a rough basis through to Monday morning, "and then we may need to reassess the situation and potentially request additional personnel."

Skip next section What was the Battle of Hürtgen Forest, the reason WWII ordnances are strewn about the area?

What was the Battle of Hürtgen Forest, the reason WWII ordnances are strewn about the area?

Friday's fire is taking place on the site of one of the longest and most costly single battles in the US military's history.

That's why the area is strewn with unexploded munitions from World War II that are at risk of exploding, both aiding the fire's spread and potentially endangering emergency services. 

The Battle of Hürtgen Forest, or Schlacht im Hürtgenwald in German, was a three-month push by US forces. They were trying at first to pin down German forces and stop them providing reinforcements in the nearby Battle of Aachen, and then later to push through the forest and advance to the Rur River.

The September-December 1944 battle tried to get through heavy fortifications as part of what the Allies knew as the Siegfried Line, a series of defensive structures that served as one of Nazi Germany's last effective lines of defense as Allied forces tried to move east toward Berlin after the D-Day landings.

Germany's military was already planning its Winter Offensive, which would be known as the Battle of the Bulge, in the same area by this point, and so its troops were given all possible resources for their defensive efforts.

The battle was seen as a comparatively rare Nazi victory in their attempts to stop the Allied advance, with at least 33,000 US casualties, and some estimates ranging considerably higher than that. Germany, with more strains on personnel and supply but also with the defenders' advantage and favorable terrain, suffered an estimated 28,000 casualties.

It's less well remembered than the much larger and more widespread Battle of the Bulge, whose main thrust was located slightly further south but in the same Eifel region. Nevertheless, it was the longest continuous battle on German ground during World War II and the second-longest single battle the US Army has ever fought.

Skip next section Cologne police launch appeal for information on fire's outbreak

Cologne police launch appeal for information on fire's outbreak

Police in the city of Cologne are investigating the cause of the Hürtgenwald fire and are appealing for help from members of the public who might be able to shed light on how it started. 

Police said in a press statement and public appeal that they had set up an online web portal where people could upload information in an "uncomplicated and direct" manner, straight to law enforcement. 

"The Cologne Police asks the public for support in the ongoing investigations. Of particular interest are clues and particularly picture or video recordings from the rough time of the start of the fire," police wrote. "Such recordings could deliver important findings and help the investigative work meaningfully."

The appeal provided a link to the site where uploads are possible, and police wrote that "any clue could be meaningful" as they seek to establish the cause of the fire.

Almost all forest fires are ultimately man-made — whether they're caused by accident or oversight or as a more deliberate act of arson.

Even in the driest and hottest summer temperatures, the heat required to trigger a fire among trees is almost never achieved by natural means — with the only plausible all-natural scenario being a lightning strike. The high summer temperatures and dry forest floor, rather than starting the fires, provide conditions suitable to enable and accelerate the spread after it's begun.

Skip next section State premier Hendrik Wüst breaking off holiday to return

State premier Hendrik Wüst breaking off holiday to return

The head of North Rhine-Westphalia's state government is breaking off his vacation to return amid the fire.

Christian Democrat politician Hendrik Wüst wanted to gather first-hand information on the situation, and told German media on Friday that he expected to reach the Düren municipality area by Saturday afternoon.

Earlier on Friday, Wüst had thanked emergency services for their work on site since Thursday afternoon, "many of them without a break," saying "out state stands together!"

Skip next section Hürtgenwald smoke can be seen, and scented, from Bonn area

Hürtgenwald smoke can be seen, and scented, from Bonn area

The plume of smoke from the Hürtgenwald, some 60 kilometers (around 35 miles) to the west, can be seen from the Rhine River here in Bonn, and particularly the hills on its right bank.

Hikers on the Petersberg summit just to the south of the city had a clear view of the smoke on Friday.

Some residents even confused the smell of smoke for a fire much closer to home.

One woman in the western district of Endenich told local public broadcaster WDR how she had called the fire service, to tell them she had reason to believe a fire had broken out in the nearby woods in Kreuzberg.

"Then the fire department told me, 'no, that really is from the Hürtgenwald. The cloud is passing over Bonn,'" she told the broadcaster. "And a minute later, a warning arrived on the NINA warning app."

NINA (the Notfall-Information und Nachrichten App) is the federal government's emergency information and news app.

Skip next section State government says fire is likely the biggest in NRW's history

State government says fire is likely the biggest in NRW's history

North Rhine-Westphalia's Agriculture Minister Silke Gorissen is visiting the area.

She said the government in Germany's most populous state is now working on the assumption that this was the largest forest fire in the state, at least in decades if not on record.

"We at least are not aware of a forest fire that reached this size," Gorissen said. "It could well be that it really is the biggest since our state was founded, and that shows what we're dealing with here."

She said she was working on the assumption that at least 200 hectares were affected but acknowledged that higher estimates were in play, saying "perhaps we're even knocking on the door of 300."

Gorissen told the dpa news agency that she could already see the smoke as she was approaching the scene.

"It really is a bit apocalyptic," she said. "It's a very imposing sight, a sad sight, seeing the forests in flame," she said.

She praised the emergency responders and the speed with which such a large multi-force response was put together.

Gorissen also appealed to people to avoid the forests in a bid to prevent any more such fires from breaking out, saying "almost all forest fires are man-made."

Skip next section IN PICTURES — Emergency services respond to Hürtgenwald wildfire

IN PICTURES — Emergency services respond to Hürtgenwald wildfire

Skip next section Fire service: 'Under no circumstances' are residents likely to return this evening

Fire service: 'Under no circumstances' are residents likely to return this evening

A firefighters' spokesman, Peter Berndgen, has told the dpa news agency that he does not expect locals in Gey to be able to return to their homes on Friday. By his estimation, Berndgen said, "under no circumstances" was this likely.

Local politician Ralf Nolten similarly suggested the evacuation could continue, saying "we need to be able to work freely," with clear roads to allow vehicles easy access to the area.

Berndgen said the efforts to extinguish the blaze could take days.

"We have very unfortunate conditions for fighting a forest fire today," he said, calling it a "red flag day" — with high temperatures, high humidity and high winds all fanning the flames.

Berndgen said specialist teams were using machine saws, tanks and other equipment to try to rapidly cut trees and form a 15-meter (49-foot) containment line around the fire, seeking to deny it the fuel it needs to spread.

Skip next section Where is the Hürtgenwald region of Germany?

Where is the Hürtgenwald region of Germany?

Skip next section Merz thanks emergency services fighting Eifel wildfires

Merz thanks emergency services fighting Eifel wildfires

Chancellor Friedrich Merz has voiced thanks to emergency services fighting the wildfires near the Dutch and Belgian borders. 

"Wildfires are burning in many parts of the country. I am being continuously updated on developments," Merz wrote in a post on social media. "Where ever it's possible, federal police and the military are providing assistance. I thank all the emergency services for their tireless endeavors, often to the point of exhaustion."

Skip next section WWII munitions complicate Eifel firefighting

WWII munitions complicate Eifel firefighting

Bundeswehr forces joined in the fight against a forest fire raging in the Eifel on Friday, adding two water transport helicopter to the operation aimed at extinguishing the Hürtgenwald blaze.

Complicating matters are the numerous munitions scattered across the area since the end of the second world war.

In an effort to safely expedite access to the area, the Bundeswehr also deployed two rescue tanks to clear munitions and cut fire roads.

"The terrain is very difficult, and because of the high concentration of ammunition," as local councilman Ralf Nolten (CDU) told Germany's dpa news agency, "we can't send individual firefighters in with firefighting backpacks," said Nolten adding, "We also heard the explosions" that went off overnight.

In the fall and winter of 1944 and 1945, the Hürtgenwald was the scene of heavy fighting between US and Nazi-German troops as US tanks sought to finish their push east into Germany to end the war.

The ferocity and scale of the fighting led US soldiers stuck there waiting for reinforcements and facing entrenched German defenses to dub it "the death factory."

entries.title: In Germany record heat meets climate action fatigue
entries.summary: For the German government climate action does not seem to be a priority — despite record temperatures, heat-related deaths and drought. Why don't more people take to the streets in protest?
entries.content:
Germany

In Germany record heat meets climate action fatigue

August 14, 2026

For the German government climate action does not seem to be a priority — despite record temperatures, heat-related deaths and drought. Why don't more people take to the streets in protest?

When Lars Werner of the "Last Generation" glued himself to the road four years ago to protest for greater climate action, Germany had not yet seen 12,500 heat-related deaths (Germany's number for 2026 so far), or record temperatures across western Europe, and fully loaded ships were still navigating the Rhine without difficulty.

"Of course, I could say 'I told you so,' because it was foreseeable and comes as no surprise whatsoever," Werner tells DW.

"The fact is, even back then, I was constantly explaining in my presentations that the Rhine would eventually run dry during hot summers and that this would have an incredible impact on the economy."

Something very strange is happening in Germany in the summer of 2026: While entire villages are being evacuated due to forest fires, farmers are losing around their harvest to drought, and hospital patients and the elderly in nursing homes face an acute threat to their lives in buildings with no air conditioning, the federal government remains astonishingly quiet.

Despite the crisis, it has still not convened a "heat summit."

"It is utterly irrational for the federal government to resort to tinkering with regulations — such as lifting the Sunday ban on truck traffic — in the hope of somehow scraping by without implementing a comprehensive climate protection policy for the long or even short term," Werner argues.

Fridays for Future Germany: not the same group from a few years ago

The government no longer has to worry about "Last Generation" protesters calling out its inaction by setting up road blockades. The climate activists halted their protests two years ago, worn down by hostility, fines and prison sentences. Now, the task of fiercely criticizing political decision-makers on climate policy falls primarily to the Fridays for Future Germany (FFF) movement.

"The federal government is doing virtually nothing when it comes to effective climate policy. Instead, various 'pseudo-solutions' are being promoted — such as dredging the Rhine to make it deeper or lifting the Sunday driving ban for trucks," FFF spokesperson Linda Kastrup told DW. She deplores what she sees as short-term fixes for the symptoms of the climate crisis, and notes that effectively nothing sustainable is being done.

Only a few hundred protesters turned out for a demonstration outside the Chancellery in Berlin a week ago. It was a far cry from the protests in 2019, prior to the COVID-19 pandemic, when hundreds of thousands of people took to the streets to demand climate action.

A recent study by the Bertelsmann Foundation found that 80% of people in Germany are worried about climate change, and more than 50% want to see more government spending on climate protection. But that doesn't mean they take to the streets.

Kastrup is not surprised.

"When Chancellor Friedrich Merz completely dismisses and ignores climate policy — when we see tens of thousands of heat-related deaths in Germany alone yet not a single word is said about it — it inevitably leaves people with the impression in their private lives that climate protection doesn't matter. Naturally, that makes it very difficult to motivate people to take to the streets," she says.

In addition, there has been a rise in hateful speech directed at climate activists on social media.

"Two days ago, I posted a reel and within a very short time, there were 2,000 hateful comments on it," says Kastrup.

Focus shifted to Ukraine, Gaza

Sebastian Haunss, a researcher in political science at the University of Bremen, says it is surprising that the scorching summer of 2026 has not led to climate protests. He finds it remarkable that on the one hand, more and more people in Germany are installing solar power systems, but on the other, they take vacations on environmentally damaging cruise ships.

He sees several reasons for this development.

"A strong counter-position has emerged," he says. "Specifically, political actors like the AfD [the far-right populist Alternative for Germany Party, Eds.] are pursuing an agenda that opposes climate protection regulations. Such actors — whether at the international or national level — did not exist just a few years ago."

Also, Haunss points out that large organizations like Fridays for Future have been replaced by a vast number of local groups, who operate largely out of the public eye. However, a pivotal event could bring people back onto the streets in large numbers at any moment, he says.

"Then there is the competition for attention; the COVID pandemic and the war in Ukraine pushed the climate issue out of the spotlight, and current economic concerns also play a major role," says Haunss, adding that many of those who took to the streets against climate change a few years ago are now focusing on different topics: "In some cases, their issues have shifted, and other topics — such as the war in Gaza and solidarity with Palestine — have moved to the forefront:"

A divided government

German Environment Minister Carsten Schneider of the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) now wants to amend the constitution, the Basic Law, to make heat protection a joint responsibility of the federal government, the states, and the municipalities. However, the larger coalition partner, the center-right bloc of the Christian Democratic Union and Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU), is skeptical and cites "legal concerns."

"Within the coalition, I do indeed see us — the SPD — as the bulwark for energy transition to renewables," Nina Scheer, energy policy spokesperson for the SPD parliamentary group, tells DW. "All my colleagues in our parliamentary group would like to achieve more in terms of climate protection. But we also have to accept setbacks regarding climate measures in order to maintain unity within the coalition."

For instance, she says, she voted in favor of making air travel cheaper and expanding regional airports, although she personally finds it wrong.

Scheer has long advocated for a faster expansion of renewable energy, and does not see eye to eye with Economics Minister Katherina Reiche (CDU), who favors gas over wind and solar power for energy supply.

"Reiche goes around pushing the narrative that while we do want climate protection and remain committed to the goals, renewables are simply too expensive. And to that, one has to say: 'No, that is simply not true,'" says Scheer.

Under the Paris Agreement and the national Climate Action Act, Germany has committed to achieving climate neutrality by 2045. However, recent statements by some politicians raise doubts as to whether the federal government is pursuing this goal with great determination.

"We cannot halt climate change from Germany alone," said Chancellor Friedrich Merz recently.

SPD politician Scheer considers this a disastrous statement.

"Fundamentally, it is a rejection of greater climate action, even though we ought to be stepping up our efforts," she says.

This article has been translated from German.

entries.title: Luigi Mangione pleads guilty to federal stalking charges in Brian Thompson death
entries.summary: The plea resolves the remaining federal charges tied to the killing of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson and could affect a separate New York state case.
entries.content:
August 14, 2026

The plea resolves the remaining federal charges tied to the killing of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson and could affect a separate New York state case.

Luigi Mangione pleaded guilty in a Manhattan federal court to stalking charges tied to the death of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson.

"I shot Mr. Thompson in Manhattan and he died," he told the court.

Prosecutors said Mangione traveled to New York City and fatally shot Thompson outside a Manhattan hotel on December 4, 2024, as he walked to UnitedHealth Group's annual investor conference.

The judge has accepted his guilty plea and said sentencing would take place in December. Mangione faces a possible sentence ‌of life without parole on the two counts of stalking.

Mangione's lawyer seeks dismissal of state murder charges

Mangione had previously pleaded not guilty to federal murder, weapons and stalking charges. Earlier this year, the judge dismissed the murder and weapons counts on legal technicalities, leaving only the stalking charges and eliminating the possibility of the death penalty.

Mangione still seperately faces murder, weapons and forgery charges in New York state court. 

Outside federal court, Mangione's lawyer, Karen Friedman Agnifilo, told reporters that "state charges must be dismissed under New York's double jeopardy protections."

Under double jeopardy protections, defendants are protected from being prosecuted for the same crime twice.

How Mangione explained his guilty plea to the court

Mangione told the federal court he pursued Thompson "after years of enduring severe pain from a broken back and navigating the obstacles of the health insurance system."

Thompson was chief executive of UnitedHealthcare, one of the largest health insurers in the United States.

He was walking into a Midtown Manhattan hotel for the annual investor day when he was shot three times in the back.

Mangione said he then used a 3D printer to make part of the gun used in the shooting.

The killing underscored widespread frustration with the US healthcare system, and some supporters portrayed Mangione as a hero.

Conservatives, including President Donald Trump, however, have called for a tough punishment.

Jamie McDonald, the Manhattan US attorney, told reporters that his office would seek a sentence of life imprisonment.

"There can be no celebrity in assassination," he said.

Outside the courthouse, a man shouted "America loves Luigi" at relatives of Thompson as they left court Friday in a convoy of black SUVs.

Thompson's family said in a statement that the plea marked an "important step toward justice."

"We look to the court to ensure that sentencing reflects the severity of this crime," the family said.

Edited by: Rob Turner

entries.title: Germany news: Car industry hemorrhaging jobs
entries.summary: The country's famed auto sector is losing jobs faster than any industrial branch in the economy, official statistics show. Meanwhile, farmers say drought conditions could affect this year's harvest. DW has more.
entries.content:
Published August 14, 2026last updated August 14, 2026

The country's famed auto sector is losing jobs faster than any industrial branch in the economy, official statistics show. Meanwhile, farmers say drought conditions could affect this year's harvest. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

This blog is now closed. Below is a roundup of top stories from and about Germany on Friday, August 14, 2026:

  • A wildfire near the Belgian border has forced around 1,800 people to leave their homes
  • Amid high temperatures, farmers say drought could badly damage grain, potato, vegetable and feed crop harvests
  • Germany's car sector is losing jobs faster than any industrial sector in the economy

For coverage of the wildfire in western Germany click on our dedicated blog here

Don't let the algorithm hide the news. If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google so you'll always see our verified news first.

Skip next section Extreme athlete arrives in Cologne after swimming from Frankfurt

Extreme athlete arrives in Cologne after swimming from Frankfurt

Nathalie Pohl has completed her four-day swin down the Main and Rhine rivers from Frankfurt to Cologne.

The 31-year-old extreme swimmer started the aquatic journey of more than 200 kilometers (124 miles) on Tuesday morning, arriving on the banks of the Rhine in Cologne on Friday afternoon.

Her aim was to raise awareness on the importance of safe swimming among children, and to fund swimming projects. Her team says they managed to raise around €616,000 ($713,000) in total.

"Every child has the right to feel secure in the water," she said upon arrival. At the same time she was keen to point out that her challenge shouldn't be taken as a "false signal."

"Especially in the Rhine, far too many people still drown," she said. "It's not bathing water."

Skip next section Germany sees rise in new business registrations

Germany sees rise in new business registrations

Germany saw a noticeable rise in new business registrations in the first half of this year. Around 352,400 new businesses were registered, up 8.3% compared with the same period last year, according to the Federal Statistical Office.

Of these, around 69,600 were considered businesses of greater economic significance — for example because of their legal form or because they planned to employ staff. That was 3.0% more than a year earlier.

At the same time, the number of complete business closures in this category fell by 3.8% to around 49,800.

Skip next section Farmers fear drought will wipe out this year's harvest

Farmers fear drought will wipe out this year's harvest

German farmers fear they could see harvests wiped out entirely by ongoing drought and unseasonably high temperatures, says German Farmers' Association (DBV) President Joachim Ruckwied.

"We expect below-average grain harvests, especially when it comes to wheat and rapeseed," he said during an interview with Germany's Redaktionsnetzwerk media group.

"As far as fall crops are concerned, the trend suggests we must expect significant yield losses here as well."

Potatoes, vegetables and sugar beets, as well as grain maize and soy could be affected.

Ruckwied warned that although farmers in the north could hope for "acceptable" if "below-average" harvests thanks to occasional rains, farmers in drier southern Germany could be facing "total harvest loss."

"What's becoming a problem, especially in southern Germany, is that feed crops aren't coming in," he added, noting that this would force farmers to slaughter animals earlier than usual.

The threat adds to the financial pressure farmers already face when it comes to buying seed, fertilizer and pesticides, says Ruckwied.

"The economic situation is brutal… on the one hand high investment costs, and on the other, lower market prices for agricultural products."

Skip next section Dramatic rescue in Berlin high-rise fire

Dramatic rescue in Berlin high-rise fire

Several people were injured Friday morning when fire broke out in a 21-story apartment complex in Berlin's Friedrichshain neighborhood, near the Ostbahnhof train station.

The blaze started on the 11th floor, say firefighters, and quickly spread to floors above.

A fire department spokesperson described the situation as "dramatic."

Witnesses say numerous residents stood at windows and balconies prepared to jump rather than be consumed by smoke and flames.

Although jump cushions were installed as a precaution below, these were not used and authorities say residents were retrieved from a stairwell with a rescue ladder.

Some 130 fire, police and emergency services personnel were in action before residents could be saved and the fire extinguished.

Smoke damage is said to have been extensive, causing at least five injuries, and leaving roughly 70 people to be cared for on site.

The cause of the fire is unclear, though police are treating it as a possible balcony fire.

Skip next section German hiker injured in Alps fall

German hiker injured in Alps fall

A 66-year old German hiker was seriously injured in a fall in the Austrian Alps on Friday according to authorities in Nesselwängle, Tyrol.

Emergency services say the man slipped and fell a few meters, losing consciousness before falling over a second, 40-meter-high (132-foot) cliff.

The man's daughter and others administered first-aid and contacted mountain rescue. He was airlifted to an Innsbruck hospital.

On Thursday, a 36-year-old German died in a fall in Zillertal, Tyrol. A few days earlier, a 74-year-old German similarly died from a fall in East Tyrol.

Skip next section Almost half of Bundestag sign up to new 'opt-out' organ donor model

Almost half of Bundestag sign up to new 'opt-out' organ donor model

More than 200 lawmakers in the lower house of parliament, the Bundestag, have signed up to a cross-party initiative seeking to change Germany's organ donor rules.

The proposal seeks to move from an "opt-in" system to an "opt-out" one. 

At present, people in Germany have to carry a donor card, register as an organ donor, or otherwise inform healthcare professionals of their willingness to donate in a legally binding manner before death. If they do not, and they are deemed potentially viable donors, sometimes their next of kin are asked to decide on their behalf — a traumatic and difficult decision in the midst of a bereavement.

With donor rates consistently failing to meet demand, some medical professionals have long advocated a system where instead of declaring your willingness to donate, you are assumed to be a potential donor unless you specifically say you are not a willing participant.

A draft law has been put forward in the Bundestag — not as a government initiative but as a cross party conscience vote, typically for causes with only a narrow chance of success but which politicians nevertheless wish to put in the spotlight.

In this case, however, 245 lawmakers have already signed the motion, in a chamber with 630 politicians. If the bill could gather some more support during the parliamentary process, it might have a chance of progressing.

Parliamentary debate on the bill is scheduled after lawmakers return from the summer break.

Around 8,000 people are currently on donor waiting lists in Germany.

Skip next section Catamaran passenger ferry crashes into Lake Constance harbor wall

Catamaran passenger ferry crashes into Lake Constance harbor wall

A catamaran passenger ferry has crashed on Lake Constance, colliding with the harbor wall.

Police said that 12 people were injured, and it was not immediately clear how seriously. They were receiving treatment on site.

Images showed that the ship had collided head-on with the harbor wall, sustaining quite considerable damage. It was still afloat, however.

Police said there was no fuel leak and no environmental hazard posed by the incident. What caused the early morning carsh was not immediately clear.

The hourly catamaran ferry brings people across Lake Constance, or the Bodensee in German, from Konstanz to Friedrichshafen.

Skip next section Car industry hemorrhaging jobs

Car industry hemorrhaging jobs

Germany's automotive branch is losing jobs faster than any industrial sector in the economy according to the Federal Statistical Office Destatis.

The car industry is second only to mechanical engineering when it comes to size, yet its employment numbers are now at their lowest since 2005.

At the end of the first half of 2026, 691,500 people were employed in Germany's leading industry, a drop of 42,300 workers, or 5.8%, within a single year.

Destatis said manufacturing employment fell by 2.7% overall but had fallen by 7.6% in the automobile sector. Smaller segments within the car sector fell by 10%, whereas manufacturers themselves registered a 6.1% drop in employment.

In May, Germany's Association of the Automobile Industry (VDA) warned that the sector stands to lose as many as 225,000 jobs by 2035.

Numerous German manufacturers, such as VW, Audi and Porsche, have all cut jobs in an effort to remain lean in the face of rising Chinese competition and punitive US tariffs.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Guten Tag from the DW newsroom in Bonn.

The major talking point on another hot, dry day in Germany is the wildfire near the Dutch and Belgian border. We've got a dedicated blog running on that story, but over here is a wrap of the other topics of the day.

Including more damaging news for the once mighty car industry, and a sharp warning from farmers on the outcome of this years crop yield.

Read on for more.

entries.title: France: Top watchdog blocks social media ban for children
entries.summary: Denying access to platforms such as Facebook, TikTok and YouTube for under-15s would infringe upon freedom of expression, the Constitutional Council has said.
entries.content:
August 14, 2026

Denying access to platforms such as Facebook, TikTok and YouTube for under-15s would infringe upon freedom of expression, the Constitutional Council has said.

France's highest constitutional authority on Friday struck down the ban on social media for children under 15.

The Constitutional Council ruled that the flagship policy of President Emmanuel Macron's second term infringed on freedom of expression.

"By prohibiting minors under the age of 15 from accessing certain online services, the law inherently requires every person, even an adult, to prove their age before accessing them," it said in its decision.

The Council is a review body that ensures laws comply with the Constitution.

Macron still wants social media ban for children

French lawmakers last month approved legislation that barred children under 15 from opening social media accounts from September 1. Beyond that, platforms would have until the start of 2027 to close children's existing accounts.

The law would also have banned the use of mobile phones in high schools and required social media platforms to introduce age-verification measures in accordance with France's privacy regulator.

The Council, however, found lawmakers had failed to set out clear rules on how people should prove their age and what limits should apply, meaning there were not enough legal safeguards in place.

Macron has instructed Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu to revise the bill to address the Constitutional Council's concerns, the Elysee Palace said. It added the president wanted the reform in place before France's 2027 presidential election.

Social media bans for teens and children also considered elsewhere

Australia became the first country in the world to ban social media for under-16s in 2025. France was the first in Europe.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen last month pledged to pursue an EU-wide social media ban for children following a recommendation by an expert group to restrict access for under-13s.

"Our children need time in the real world. Time to play, time to build friendships, time to make mistakes. Time to shape their own identity, their own personality, before an algorithm shapes them instead," von der Leyen told reporters in Brussels.

"This is not about whether children can access social media. It is about whether and when social media can access our children," she said.

A number of other countries have announced plans to consider similar bans, including Brazil, the UK, Canada, Norway and Denmark.

Edited by: Rob Turner
